title: Tu BiShvat: planting
hook: many plant trees or give to planting on this day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mystics' Tu BiShvat seder, with its fruits and four cups. Your line was fruits of the tree. Today, the other half of the day: putting a tree in the ground.

A man walking along a road sees someone planting a carob tree. He stops and asks: how long until this tree bears fruit? Seventy years, comes the answer. The traveler looks him up and down. And you're sure you'll be alive in seventy years to eat from it? The planter keeps digging. That's a story from the Talmud, in tractate Taanit. The traveler is Choni, whom the same page remembers for praying down rain, and his story goes on to become something like Rip Van Winkle. But the planter's answer is the part people quote.
screen: `A MAN PLANTS A CAROB.` → `SEVENTY YEARS TO FRUIT.` → `WILL YOU BE ALIVE TO EAT IT?`

segments.voice: The planter says, roughly: I found this world full of carob trees. My ancestors planted them for me, so I'm planting for my children. Then Choni sits down to eat, falls asleep, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that very tree. Are you the one who planted it? No, the man says: my grandfather did. That's the Talmud's picture of planting: you do it for someone you may never meet. The midrash finds the same idea in the Torah's command to plant fruit trees when Israel enters the land. Even God, it notes, began the world by planting: Genesis says God planted a garden in Eden. So planting becomes a way of imitating God. Another teaching, in a collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan, is bolder still. It's attributed to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: if you're holding a sapling in your hand and someone tells you the Messiah has arrived, plant the sapling first. Then go out to greet him. Tu BiShvat became a planting day only in modern times. The story usually told is that a teacher in the village of Zikhron Yaakov took his students out to plant trees on the fifteenth of Shevat, and the custom spread through schools and, later, tree-planting campaigns. Today some people plant on this day, and others give money for planting. In the northern winter it's often too cold to dig, so people plant indoors, or give, or water what's already growing. Somebody planted for you.
screen: `MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME.` · `CHONI SLEEPS SEVENTY YEARS.` · `GOD PLANTED A GARDEN FIRST.` · `PLANT THE SAPLING, THEN GO.` · then, large: `PLANT SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: If there's a plant near you, give it water now, slowly, and watch the soil drink; if not, picture a tree you've loved and whoever planted it. Then think of one person who planted something for you: a lesson, a habit, a kindness you're still eating from.
Tu BiShvat. The new year for trees, and in modern times, a day for planting what others will enjoy. Today's word.
Your line: plant something. The fruit may well go to someone you'll never meet. Day six hundred seventy-one, done.

howItsDone: Many Jews plant trees on Tu BiShvat, especially in Israel, where schools hold planting days; elsewhere many give to tree-planting funds, eat fruits of the land, or care for plants at home.

chat.says: Why plant a tree if you won't be around to eat its fruit?
options: Someone planted for you, so you plant for others, like the carob planter in the Talmud.
You shouldn't; the Talmud says to plant only what you will harvest yourself.
It's about the date: plant on Tu BiShvat and the tree is sure to be blessed.
chat.meaning: In the Talmud the carob planter says his ancestors planted for him, so he plants for his children: for someone he may never meet.
